analysis.one_liner: Excludes assets sold through investment contracts, including digital tokens, from securities laws.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote; it sat in the House Financial Services Committee until the Congress ended with 3 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend five federal securities laws to say that an asset sold under an "investment contract" — the legal category that covers most cryptocurrency fundraising — is not itself a security. Today, courts treat the contract as a security, which triggers registration, disclosure, and anti-fraud rules from the Securities and Exchange Commission. Under this bill, the tokens sold would be outside those rules. It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Cryptocurrency firms and token issuers gain the most: they could raise money by selling digital tokens without registering the offering with the SEC or making the disclosures securities law requires, and the assets could trade without exchange-registration obligations. Venture-backed blockchain projects and trading platforms would also face fewer legal constraints.

how_it_helps.text: Codifies in statute that an asset sold pursuant to an investment contract is not a security, so token sales would not need SEC registration or public disclosure.
Expresses the sense of Congress that the current approach has "discouraged development of the digital asset sector" and states a purpose of removing that treatment for digital assets.

Amends five securities statutes at once — the Securities Act, the Advisers Act, the Investment Company Act, the Exchange Act, and the investor-protection law — so the exemption applies across registration, adviser, investment-company, and broker-dealer rules.

analysis.who_pays: Retail investors buying digital tokens would bear the cost. They would lose the registration, disclosure, and anti-fraud protections the securities laws provide when they put money into a venture run by the promoter, with no replacement protections created.

drawbacks.text: The bill provides no substitute disclosure or anti-fraud regime for token offerings, so investors in projects run by promoters would lose the protections that securities registration and liability rules provide.

The exemption is written broadly — it covers any tangible or intangible asset sold under an investment contract, not just digital tokens — so courts would have to decide how far the carve-out reaches beyond cryptocurrency.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill creates a clear rule for one fast-growing industry, which supporters argue is fair because courts historically treated the asset (like the orange groves in the Howey case) as separate from the investment contract. But the trade-off falls on ordinary buyers: the securities framework it removes is the main source of mandatory disclosure and fraud liability for token offerings, and the bill replaces it with nothing. Whether the clarity outweighs losing those protections depends largely on how much one trusts token issuers to disclose voluntarily.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never brought it up before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Emmer introduced the bill on July 16, 2021, joined by Reps. Darren Soto and Ro Khanna as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day of introduction and received no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in its action history.
The bill ended the 117th Congress with 3 cosponsors and never advanced out of committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Retail buyers of digital tokens are better off because the bill died: the SEC's existing authority to treat token fundraising as investment contracts under the Howey framework remains in place, along with its registration and anti-fraud leverage. Crypto issuers did not obtain the exemption they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Retail crypto investors kept SEC protections

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican with two Democratic cosponsors, but the bill never reached a vote, so the chamber's partisan split on it was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would have let token issuers raise money without SEC registration or disclosure, cutting their compliance costs. The gain comes directly at the expense of the retail investors who fund those projects, who would lose the legal protections that come with a security.

Buyers of digital tokens sold through investment contracts would no longer get the registration, disclosure, and fraud-liability rules that apply to securities, with no replacement protections in the bill.
